newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French shares dip on conflicting poll rumours.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French shares dip on conflicting poll rumours.

text.p: The French share market lost early gains on Thursday, buffeted by rumours of conflicting private opinion polls about Sunday's election runoff, while a spat over Bundesbank gold drew attention away, dealers said.

The share market has fallen more than six percent over the last three days as investors began to take more seriously the prospect of a left-wing win in the election. It stabilised on Thursday as dealers felt Wednesday's losses were excessive.
The rise was underpinned by a rumour about an opinion poll putting right-wing parties in a strong position after a series of rumoured private polls saying the left was well placed.
The publication of opinion polls was banned in France from one week before last Sunday's first round, in which the left scored an unexpected win over the ruling centre-right coalition.

A California-based internet site published three polls which indicated strong showings for the left while a Swiss-based French language paper is set to publish a poll on Thursday evening which is rumoured to indicate the opposite.
"It's a market of excesses. There have been enormous swings but they do not mean much. On top of that, the dollar is up and the international situation is not bad," a broker said.
The dollar was boosted by a flow of funds out of the mark in the wake of a spat between the Bundesbank and the Bonn government over the revaluation of Bundesbank gold.

At 1200 GMT, the blue-chip CAC-40 index was up 0.13 percent at 2586.61. It hit a high of 2,627.54 and a low of 2,580.62. Volume was a brisk 4.6 billion francs after having reached a total of 12.45 billion francs for one of the highest daily turnover figures on Wednesday.
The index closed at 2,522.67 on Monday April 21 before President Jacques Chirac called the snap election.
French bond futures were also mostly unmoved on Thursday as election jitters kept investors wary. "Investors are reluctant to get into this market," said a trader.

French 10-year bonds were yielding nine points less than German paper, unchanged from Wednesday. The franc traded at 3.3788 against the mark, up from Wednesday's 3.3816 but still below its pre-election level of around 3.36 per mark.
Bond traders said they believed that whatever the outcome of the Sunday election, France's position towards European Monetary Union (EMU) would be largely the same.

"During an election campaign, people focus on the normal right-left debate, but all politicians who get close to power are caught into a funnel which takes them towards the single currency. Nobody dares to torpedo that," a trader said.
French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin told the Le Monde newspaper on Thursday that his party backed Europe's planned single currency and that this would be the position of a left-wing government.
"We are for the single currency, since the ouset. One can be against the single currency and that's a respectable stance but it would not be the position of a government," he said.
Outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who said on Monday he would not return to office even if the right-wing won on Sunday, on Thursday warned against a victory by the left.

"We will get it for five years," he said about a possible "cohabitation" between a left-wing government and Gaullist Chirac. "We must think what France will look like in the year 2000 according to whether we have a Socialist-Communist-Green majority or an RPR-UDF majority," he said.
